chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
title: Playing tangos at the Arcadia
summary: Roy had to learn dance music, got help from Paul Martell, and learned to play mellow dance sets.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: The first Sunday we played there, the first week, I had to play the tango compositions. And I had never had no dealings with tangos, but my brother and Prince Robinson did, because they had been in New York, and they played dancing schools and they knew all about that. I didn't even know how to start it off, to tell you the truth. So Joe said, "Just give us a downbeat, we'll take it," you know. Let's see, I think Sidney Catlett was playing drums with me at first, when we first went in there. Yeah, I'm pretty sure he was. It was Sidney or Beason, Bill Beason. Sidney! What year did Chick die? '39?

It was Sidney, yeah. That's the year we went in. So we got it straight... No, Paul Martell was the other band. All these people that was doing the tango, they was giving me hell, you know. And actually, what really sold me on the gig after he got with me, he came up to me and said, "Listen, Roy. I have a lot of orchestrations of tangos and Viennese waltzes [and I didn't have none of that!] and the rhumbas and things like this, things for (?), and I'll give them to you, but as a friend. I know you cats are great. So as a friend, let me rehearse your band on the tangos."
So that got me very happy. And he rehearsed us and got us straight with a few tangos and things, you know.

Then one night I was just feeling like a little let down, you know, and I said, "Shit." So I played "Whispering" with the soft mute, you know, nice tempo, and the boss comes and said, "That's it." He said, "Now, if you play numbers like that, that's what people can consistently dance on. You know, later on... You can't just play that Jazz straight through." So from then on, I knew how to play it, you know.

Then on Sunday, we had one set where we could play anything we wanted, and then went hog wild for that one set. Near the end of the set, the guy, old McDonald I called him, he just caught me and give me this. That meant two waltzes and two tangos! That was the end of the Swing!
And we got air time down there, too; again, we got air time, you know. That was a good band, though. Don made some helluva arrangements on that band. Pshew! I just wish I had that book again.
